RAB_MONSTER_NUMBERS_BONUS: Each of your %PRACE% gets RB_MonsterNumbersBonus_Power for every enemy monster in play.
RAB_VAMPIREPOWER_BONUS: %PRACE% permanently gain RB_VampireBonus_Power and RB_VampireBonus_Health when they kill a creature.
RAB_BLOODSUCKER_BONUS: %PRACE% permanently gain RB_BloodSuckerUp_Health when they take @X

RAB_RUNEHEALTH_BONUS: All of your %PRACE% permanently gain RB_RuneBonus_Health when you play a rune.
RAB_ELEMENTAL_BONUS: All of your %PRACE% permanently gain RB_ElementalBonus_Power and RB_ElementalBonus_Health when you play a spell.
RAB_WEREWOLF_BONUS: %PRACE% permanently gain RB_WerewolfBonus_Health when they kill an enemy creature.
RAB_ZOMBIE_BONUS: All %PRACE% permanently gain RB_ZombieBonus_Health when any creature dies.
RAB_ZOMBIEPOWER_BONUS: All %PRACE% permanently gain RB_ZombieBonus_Power when any creature dies.
RAB_ORC_BONUS: Each of your %PRACE% gets RB_OrcBonus_Power for each of your other %PRACE% in play.
RAB_ELF_BONUS: All of your %PRACE% get RB_ElfBonus_Health while you have no other races in play.
RAB_MINOTAUR_BONUS: %PRACE% permanently gain RB_MinotaurBonus_Power and RB_MinotaurBonus_Health each time they are (re)equipped.
RAB_DWARF_BONUS: %PRACE% permanently gain RB_DwarfBonus_Power when they survive an attack by another creature.

RAB_FREINDLY_DEATH_GAINS_POWER: Each of your %PRACE% permanently gains RB_FriendlyDeathBonus_Power when another of your monsters dies.

RAB_MOBARMOUR_BONUS: %PRACE% get RB_Mob_Armour for each adjacent friendly monster.

HELP_GAMEPLAY_1:
Each player has to bring a hero into combat, the objective being to control the last one alive.

When your hero dies, that's game over for you, so try to keep it safe.

You can attack enemies with your hero, but the safer option is to spawn monsters and let them do your fighting.
HELP_GAMEPLAY_2:
Monsters will form the backbone of your strategy to winning in combat - the clue is in the game title!

You can deploy monsters into combat during your own turn, but keep in mind that it's your hero who calls them forth, which means monsters can only be spawned on an empty space adjacent to your hero.

Use your spawned monsters to attack your enemies, but try to remember that whilst killing the enemy's hordes can be fun, you only have to kill their hero to win the battle.
HELP_GAMEPLAY_3:
Prior to starting a battle, you need to make a "deck". All of the various monsters and other items exist in card form, and it is your job to mix these cards together into a coherent deck.

This deck is shuffled at the start of combat and you then draw an initial "hand" of six cards. You also draw one card at the start of each of your turns*.

On your own turn, you can then play these cards onto the battlefield to spawn monsters etc.

(* Because going first can otherwise give a slight advantage, the starting player does not draw an additional card on their first turn.)
HELP_GAMEPLAY_4: Every card has a Mojo cost required to play it. If you don't have enough Mojo at the time, you will not be able to do so. This cost can be seen as a purple number at the top/left of all card imagery.\n\nYou can earn Mojo in various ways, but your Hero conveniently generates Mojo for you at the start of your turn - exactly how much depends upon the Hero you pick.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_1:
Monsters are the bread and butter of the game, and we recommend you fill at least a third of your deck with them.

Each monster card spawns a real life monster onto the battlefield, but that monster's various powers and abilities all come from what's written on the card.

Tap and hold on any battlefield monster during combat and you will be shown a large view of the monster card plus any extra cards for equipped items, etc.

Below is a description of everything you will see on the large card view for a monster, and how it relates to gameplay.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_2: This is how much power your monster starts off with. When it performs any kind of attack, it is this value that is used to determine the amount of damage dealt to the victim.\n\nThere are many in-combat modifiers for a monster's power at any one moment, but the card view will always show just the starting value.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_3:
This is how much health (or life) your monster starts off with.

When attacked, the attacker's power is subtracted from the victim's health. When a monster's health drops to zero, well - you can figure out what happens to it next!

There are many in-combat modifiers for a monster's health at any one moment, but the card view will always show just the starting value.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_4:
All cards, not just monsters, have a rarity icon. This does not directly affect any in-combat statistics, but is an indicator of how regularly a given card will show up in a booster chest.

It stands to reason though that the rarer the card, the generally better it will be.

The categories of rareness are:
@J
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_5: All cards have a Mojo cost required to play them. You earn this Mojo in many different ways, the most direct of which being your hero, who generates some at the start of each of your turns.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_6: There are many different races of monster in the game. Each monster belonging to a particular race will receive that race's bonus in combat, all the time, as a passive ability.\n\nThese racial bonuses are specifically designed to encourage certain deck-building strategies, but working with different races in the same deck can develop a near infinite number of fun combinations of deck synergy.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_7: A lot of monsters, but not all, come with their own specialised skill beyond a basic attack. If they have one, it will be described on the card.\n\nDuring combat you may select these additional abilities instead of performing a basic attack, provided you have the Mojo to pay for it.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_8:
A monster's name should be obvious enough, but its class merits further explanation.

There are four different classes of monster within each race, Warriors, Archers, Mages and Artillery. Each of these classes have signature abilities, for example Warriors tend to have more Power and Health, whereas Archers are generally weaker but can fire further.

The most important thing to note though, is that you have to match the various weapons cards to their owner's class. You cannot put a bow on a Mage, nor can you put a Mages Staff on a Warrior. Etc.

Weapons and their use is described in more detail under the "Other Cards" topic.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_9:
Warrior class creatures have an attack range of 1.
This means that they must be directly adjacent to the target to perform a basic attack or use an activated ability on it.

As an added bonus, warrior monsters can take an additional move at the expense of not attacking on that turn.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_10: Mage class creatures have an attack range of 1 - 2.\n\nThis means they can attack or use their ability on any valid target that is either adjacent or one space away from them.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_11: Archer class creatures have an attack range of 2 - 3.\n\nThis means they can attack or use their ability on any valid target that is two or three spaces away. Note that they cannot fire at "point blank" range.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_12: Artillery class creatures have an attack range of 3.\n\nThis means they can attack any valid target that is exactly three spaces away. Note that they cannot both attack and move on the same turn.
HELP_MONSTERCARDS_13: Some activated abilities don't use a creature for a target, but select a map space for some sort of area effect.\n\nIn these cases you will be shown the valid locations you can pick, and the card will describe the range and effect of the ability.
HELP_OTHERCARDS_1:
Apart from the obvious Monsters, there are several different core types of cards you might want to put in your deck.

Each of these types bring different benefits, and a well constructed deck will usually feature at least a few cards from each.

Because screen space is limited, cards come in two sizes. Most of the time you will see an abbreviated smaller version, but if you tap and hold on one, a larger view will be presented.
HELP_OTHERCARDS_2:
As there are four different classes of monster - Warriors, Archers, Mages and Artillery - there are also four classes of weapon to go with them.

You will note that the different classess of monster cards have uniquely coloured backgrounds, and these are repeated on the their matching weapons cards.

Mages may only be equipped with Staffs, Archers may only be equipped with Bows, whilst Warriors can use all the rest, referred to as "Melee Weapons"

Every weapon has a Power "buff", noted in the top/right corner, that adds to its bearer's Power for as long as the weapon is in hand.

Some weapons may do other things as well, such as causing an Affliction on the defender.
HELP_OTHERCARDS_3:
Armour cards can be played onto your own spawned monsters that are already on the battlefield.

Like most cards, armour can bring other benefits as well, but the main thing they do is give your monster some defence.

Defence (Shields and Armour) works similarly to health in that it absorbs damage. When an attack comes in, damage is dealt to the defence first, and only if there is any surplus does the remainder get applied to the defending monster's health.

For example, if a monster with 2 Health and 2 Defence is attacked by a monster with 3 Power, the first 2 Power goes into the defence and the remaining 1 Power then gets taken off the defender's health. It just escaped with it's life!

Once a shield has absorbed it's fill in damage, it no longer functions until the start of your next turn, at which time it is fully recharged.
HELP_OTHERCARDS_4: Shields function in the same way as armour and are collectively referred to as "defence". Graphically, a shield will appear on an equipped monster's arm, whereas armour appears as a helmet, chest plate and shoulder pads ensemble.\n\nBecause defence is always a good thing, you are allowed to equip a monster with both a shield and some armour should you wish.
HELP_OTHERCARDS_5:
Spells all have some sort of instant effect on the battle.

These effects vary a lot, such as dealing damage to monsters, drawing extra cards, getting more mojo, etc.

You will have to read each card to see what's available, but a well timed spell can turn a battle.

To cast a global spell, simply drag the card from your hand anywhere onto the battlefield. For targetted spells, drag over a valid target, which will light up in the usual way, and let go whilst over it.
HELP_OTHERCARDS_6:
Runes are the "permanently on" version of spells, and generally provide for similar types of effects.

For example a spell to draw two cards will work just the once, whereas a rune to draw a card will draw a card at the start of each of your turns, indefinitely - full details will be written on the card.

Because runes are more powerful than spells, you are limited to how many you can have in play at once.

To play a rune you must drop it onto the Rune Stand of your own colour, of which there are typically two to four in total, based on the battlefield layout.

(In skirmish or online games, there are always exactly four.)

You can play a new rune over an old one to replace it. (Doing so does not count as destroying it.)

Like monsters, runes have health (they all start at RUNICSTARTHEALTH) and can be attacked by creatures. Once a rune's health is reduced to zero, it is destroyed and disappears. Note that to attack a rune, the attacking monster must be stood adjacent to the rune regardless of its class.

The casting cost for a rune is face value mojo plus 2 more for each similar rune already in play under your control.
HELP_DECKRULES_1:
There are five different sets of deck rules, as listed below. For any type of game (online, skirmish, etc.), you may pick a set of deck rules, and all participants must bring a suitable deck to adhere to them.

The single player quests can be played through four times for prizes, once with each set of rules, but you must first unlock the others by completing the quest with Standard rules.

NB:
In the campaigns, please note that whilst you have to stick to those deck rules, the AI does not.
HELP_DECKRULES_2:
This should be considered the "normal" way to play the game.

Your deck must contain between 30 and 200 cards, with no greater than four copies of any one card.

Foils do not count as being different from plain versions of the same card - you may mix and match foils and plain but no greater than four in any combination is allowed.
HELP_DECKRULES_3: Your deck must contain exactly 50 cards, no more and no less, and with no duplicate cards at all - all 50 cards must be different.
HELP_DECKRULES_4:
Tribal adheres to the same rules as Standard, with the following additions:

1) Each deck must contain exactly one race of monsters, no more and no less.

2) Monsters must account for a minimum of 60% of all the cards in the deck.
HELP_DECKRULES_5: Pauper also adheres to the same rules as Standard, with the following single addition:\n\nYou may not use any rare or legendary cards. All cards in the deck must be of common or uncommon rarity only.
HELP_DECKRULES_6: Hordes also adheres to the same rules as Standard, with the following single addition:\n\nYou may use ONLY monster cards in your deck. Nothing else!
FACT_POWER_TILE: Your creature just walked onto a power tile. It will get an attack power boost for as long as it stays on it.
HELP_AFF_1:
"Affliction" is a catch-all term for any lasting effects an attack might leave on a creature. They will either last one round or forever, and fall into one of two categories - good and bad.

Some spells and abilities might act to remove a particular affliction, whilst others might act on good or bad ones collectively.

Remember that any creature stepping on to a regen tile will have all bad afflictions cured instantly.
